pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 9–11; the cryosphere and its role in Earth's water system — the cryosphere is all of Earth's frozen water (ice sheets, glaciers, sea ice, permafrost, snow cover); the polar ice sheets store roughly 68–69% of Earth's fresh water; if all land ice melted, sea level would rise more than ~65 metres; and the water cycle links polar ice to the whole planet through evaporation, precipitation and meltwater flowing to the oceans.
• Standards—UK: DfE KS2 Y4 'States of matter' (the water cycle) extended; KS3 Chemistry 'Earth and atmosphere' and geography (water/carbon stores).
• Standards—US: NGSS 5-ESS2-1/-2 (interacting Earth systems; where water is found) and MS-ESS2-4 (water cycle driven by energy and gravity).
• Operational details: two ideas — (1) the cryosphere as a NAMED part of the Earth system with distinct components (ice sheets, glaciers, sea ice, permafrost, snow), holding most of the planet's fresh water; and (2) it is a live STORE connected to oceans and atmosphere by the water cycle, so changes there ripple globally (sea level, currents, water supply). Use proportions (most fresh water is frozen; most of THAT is in Antarctica) and the striking 'if it all melted' figure. Distinguish frozen freshwater stores (raise sea level when melted) from floating sea ice.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (9) name three parts of the cryosphere; Tier B (10) state that most of Earth's fresh water is frozen in the ice sheets; Tier C (11) explain how the cryosphere connects to oceans and atmosphere via the water cycle and why melting land ice raises sea level.
bestPractices: Introduce 'cryosphere' as a single umbrella term and enumerate its components so it is concrete, not jargon
Use proportion visuals (fresh vs salt water; frozen vs liquid fresh water) to land 'most fresh water is frozen'
Connect the store to flows — evaporation, snowfall, glaciers, meltwater to the sea — so it's part of the water cycle, not an isolated block
Reuse the sea-ice vs land-ice distinction: only melting land-based frozen water adds to the oceans
Anchor the 'if it all melted' figure to make the scale of the store vivid, while noting it is a thought experiment
keyRepresentations: Cryosphere component map: ice sheets, glaciers, sea ice, permafrost, snow cover
Water-store proportion bars: salt vs fresh, and frozen vs liquid fresh water
Water-cycle diagram with the cryosphere as a store feeding oceans/atmosphere
'If all land ice melted' sea-level rise scale (~65 m) against a familiar skyline
commonMisconceptions: Most of Earth's fresh water is in rivers and lakes — the great majority is frozen in ice sheets and glaciers
The cryosphere is just 'ice at the poles' — it also includes glaciers, permafrost, snow cover and sea ice worldwide
Frozen water is separate from the water cycle — it is a major store connected by evaporation, snowfall and meltwater
Melting any ice raises sea level equally — only land ice adds water; floating sea ice does not raise it
The ice is a permanent, unchanging block — it constantly exchanges water with oceans and atmosphere

learn.summary: For ages 9–11: learners build an understanding of the cryosphere as all of Earth's frozen water (ice sheets, glaciers, sea ice, permafrost, snow cover), grasp that most of Earth's fresh water is frozen (polar ice sheets hold roughly 68–69% per cited sources), and learn that the cryosphere is a live store connected to oceans and atmosphere through the water cycle. A central discriminating idea: melting land-based ice is what raises sea level noticeably, because floating sea ice already displaces its own weight of water (in the real salty ocean, melting sea ice adds only a very tiny rise). Activities range from a manipulable store-and-flow model and a labelled component map to a hands-on displacement demonstration and a companion recognition/estimate check.

activities.title: Frozen Earth console: melt it and watch the system respond
feedback: If a learner expects floating sea ice to raise the gauge: point out the gauge held still, and connect this to displacement — floating ice already pushes aside its own weight of water.
If a learner names only polar ice caps: revisit the component map so glaciers, permafrost, snow cover and sea ice are seen as one worldwide system.
Reinforce the proportion bars: the tiny frozen sliver holds most of Earth's fresh water — not rivers and lakes.
activities.rationale: A store wired into flows is made concrete when learners operate it and see proportions, connections, and the land-vs-sea-ice rule as consequences of their actions rather than as told facts. The optional linked gauge, proportion bars and live water-cycle arrows make the mechanism visible. This is one effective medium, not the only way to teach these ideas; the figures it presents are the sourced figures below.
sourceClaims: The polar ice sheets store roughly 68–69% of Earth's fresh water
If both polar ice sheets melted entirely, global sea level would rise by more than 65 metres (Greenland ~7.4 m + Antarctica ~58 m)
learnerActions: Study a display of the planet's water as two proportion bars — a large salty-sea bar and, within the small fresh-water sliver, a bar showing that most fresh water is frozen.
Explore a map of cryosphere components: ice sheets, glaciers, sea ice, permafrost, and snow cover.

Melt components one at a time and observe a sea-level gauge: melting floating Arctic sea ice leaves the gauge still; melting the Greenland and Antarctic ice SHEETS makes it climb toward a marked ~65 m level (per cited sources: Greenland ~7.4 m + Antarctica ~58 m).
Watch water-cycle arrows respond as you act — evaporation, snowfall rebuilding glaciers, and meltwater rivers flowing to the sea — showing ice as a live store, not a static block.
State in your own words why the frozen sliver matters and why only land ice lifts the sea.
activities.intendedInsight: The cryosphere is a giant connected reservoir holding most of Earth's fresh water; it exchanges water with oceans and atmosphere through the water cycle, and only land-based ice raises sea level when it melts.

activities.title: Cryosphere map and water-store proportion bars
feedback: If a learner says most fresh water is in rivers and lakes: use the frozen-vs-liquid bar to show the great majority is frozen.
If only 'poles' are named: point to glaciers, permafrost and snow cover on the map as part of the same system.
activities.rationale: A labelled map plus proportion bars teaches the parts and the 'most fresh water is frozen' figure clearly. It is a good scaffold for the vocabulary and proportions; on its own it does not show the dynamic melt-to-sea-level and water-cycle linkage, which the console activity adds.
sourceClaims: The polar ice sheets store roughly 68–69% of Earth's fresh water
learnerActions: Label a component map identifying ice sheets, glaciers, sea ice, permafrost and snow cover.
Examine proportion bars for salt vs fresh water, and frozen vs liquid fresh water; optionally tap-to-reveal the key figures.
State which store holds most of Earth's fresh water and name three parts of the cryosphere.
activities.intendedInsight: The cryosphere is a named umbrella term with distinct components worldwide, and most of Earth's fresh water is frozen in the ice sheets and glaciers.

activities.title: Displacement demo: floating ice vs land ice
feedback: If a learner predicts the floating cube overflows: run the demo; if the level stays about the same (allowing for small spills or condensation), this shows the floating ice was already displacing its own weight of water.
If a learner thinks melt creates NEW water: connect to states of matter — the same water changes state and location; mass is conserved.
Prompt further thinking: scientists still care about shrinking Arctic sea ice for reasons beyond sea level (e.g. reflecting sunlight, habitat) — invite the learner to reason about why.
Note the limit of the analogy: the spoon/saucer cube isolates displacement only; real land ice melt is driven by many factors, so the demo shows the sea-level rule, not the full cause of melting.
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–explain demonstration surfaces the common 'all melting ice raises sea level' misconception and lets the learner test it directly, grounding the displacement reasoning that distinguishes floating from land ice.
learnerActions: Fill a glass to the brim with water and float an ice cube in it.

Predict, WITH A REASON, whether the glass will overflow as the floating cube melts, then let it melt and observe whether the level changes (it should stay at about the same level; wipe the outside of the glass so condensation is not mistaken for overflow).
Let meltwater from a cube resting on a spoon or saucer lip (standing for land ice) run into the glass, and observe that this overflows.
Compare the two cases and explain why floating ice behaves differently from land ice.
Transfer to a new case: decide whether Greenland's land ice or floating Arctic sea ice matters more for rising seas, and say why.
activities.intendedInsight: Floating ice already displaces its own weight of water, so in this fresh-water demo melting it keeps the level about the same (in the salty ocean, melting sea ice adds only a very tiny rise); land-based ice adds new water to the sea. Mass is conserved — melting changes state and location, not the amount of water.

activities.title: Companion check: name, estimate, and distinguish
feedback: For land-vs-sea-ice items, follow a correct or incorrect choice by asking the learner to give the displacement reason, not just the answer.
Use incorrect estimates as a cue to revisit the proportion bars.
activities.rationale: Recognition and estimate tasks make a solid check on the taught ideas. They can assess and reinforce the vocabulary and distinction, but recognition alone does not by itself elicit the learner's independent construction of displacement reasoning, so they work best alongside the model and demo rather than replacing them.
learnerActions: Name three parts of the cryosphere.
Use a proportion estimate (e.g. a slider) to indicate how much of Earth's fresh water is frozen.
Answer land-vs-sea-ice questions about which melting ice raises sea level and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates the vocabulary, the proportion figure, and the land-vs-sea-ice distinction.

activities.title: Glaciologist's account of the cryosphere (optional discussion)
feedback: Draw out the land-vs-sea-ice distinction in discussion and ask the learner to explain displacement in their own words.
Follow factual claims with a 'why' so the learner reasons rather than recalls.
activities.rationale: A narrated account with responsive discussion can introduce the system and its vocabulary and prompt reasoning. For the store-and-flow behaviour specifically, a manipulable model or hands-on demo gives learners something to operate; discussion complements these rather than substituting for them.
learnerActions: Listen to or read a short account of the cryosphere's components and its role connecting ice to oceans and atmosphere.
Ask questions and respond: where is most frozen water, and why does only land ice raise the sea?
activities.intendedInsight: The cryosphere is a connected store at the heart of the water cycle; changes there ripple globally to sea level, currents and water supply.

constraints: Introduce 'cryosphere' as a single umbrella term and enumerate its components so it is concrete rather than jargon.
Distinguish frozen freshwater stores on land (raise sea level when melted) from floating sea ice (does not raise sea level in this teaching model).
Treat the '~65 m if all land ice melted' figure as a thought experiment used to convey scale, not a prediction of events; scope it to melting land ice sheets, not floating sea ice.
The recognition/estimate check assesses and reinforces understanding but does not by itself elicit the independent construction of displacement reasoning; pair it with the demo or model.
The labelled map and proportion bars are a scaffold for vocabulary and figures; they do not demonstrate the dynamic melt-to-sea-level or water-cycle linkage on their own.
Any flat diagram or screen model represents the real 3D Earth system; name it as a model when comparing proportions and flows.
Connect the store to its flows (evaporation, snowfall, glaciers, meltwater to the sea) so the cryosphere is understood as part of the water cycle, not an isolated block.
Present the cited figures (68–69%; >65 m) as sourced but unverified; no source establishes the comparative efficacy or necessity of any one activity medium.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources have NOT been re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

All four source claims are marked verified:false in the row; the 68–69% fresh-water figure and the >65 m (Greenland ~7.4 m + Antarctica ~58 m) sea-level figure are attributed to NSIDC/Copernicus but are unverified here — present as sourced figures, not independently confirmed.

Source claims attached to activities document the figures/curriculum coverage those activities present; they do not support any medium-efficacy claim in a rationale, and none establishes comparative efficacy or necessity among media.

The original medium-comparison rationales included efficacy-style phrasing ('best learned by operating it', 'better manipulated than discussed'); these have been softened to scoped proposals, as the sources do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity among media.
The spoon/saucer 'land ice' analogy is an approximation: real land ice melt is driven by many factors; the demo isolates displacement only. This limit is now stated in the demo activity itself.

The teaching model 'floating sea ice melt does not raise sea level' omits the small salinity/density effect; it matches the original and is acceptable at this age but is a simplification, not an exact physical result.

Self-audit: arithmetic Greenland ~7.4 m + Antarctica ~58 m sums to ~65.4 m, consistent with the '>65 m' claim; displacement physics (floating ice displaces its own weight, so melting holds a brim-full level) is sound as stated for fresh water.

assess.poeTask: Fill a glass to the brim with water and float an ice cube in it; ask the child to predict, WITH A REASON, whether it will overflow as the cube melts. The naive prediction ('it'll overflow because the ice adds water') is the diagnostic part. Let it melt — the level holds. Then let meltwater from a cube resting on a spoon lip (standing for land ice) run in, to show that overflows.
probeDeeper: About how much of the world's fresh water is locked up as ice, and what would it mean for rivers and drinking water if it all melted?
Greenland's ice sits on land; most Arctic sea ice floats. Which one should we worry about for rising seas, and why?
If floating ice doesn't raise the sea when it melts, why do scientists still care about Arctic sea ice shrinking?
What if the glass wasn't full to the brim — would the floating cube change your answer about the sea?
assess.correctAnswer: The floating ice cube will NOT make the glass overflow — floating ice already pushes aside (displaces) exactly its own weight of water, so when it melts it just fills the space it was displacing and the level stays the same. The ice on the saucer stands for land ice (glaciers and ice sheets on land): if its meltwater ran into the glass it WOULD raise the level. So only melting LAND ice raises sea level; melting floating sea ice does not.

errorPatterns.pattern: all melting ice raises sea level — 'the sea ice at the North Pole melting is what floods coasts'
errorPatterns.nextMove: run the glass demo; floating ice displaces its weight so the level holds; only land ice adds water
errorPatterns.distractor: The floating cube overflows the glass, because melted ice adds more water
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the floating cube overflows the glass

errorPatterns.pattern: the cryosphere is just the poles — doesn't count mountain glaciers, snow cover, permafrost or sea ice as one system
errorPatterns.nextMove: map the cryosphere: sea ice, ice sheets, glaciers, snow, permafrost, frozen lakes
errorPatterns.revealedBy: names only polar ice caps when asked what frozen water Earth has

errorPatterns.pattern: frozen water is 'not really' water — reasons that melt adds NEW water rather than the same water changing state
errorPatterns.nextMove: link to states of matter; mass is conserved, only state and location change
errorPatterns.revealedBy: reasons melt creates extra water instead of the same water changing state and location

responseLevels.gap: Says both melting cubes overflow, or that all polar melt raises the sea; treats frozen water only as 'the ice caps'.
responseLevels.full: Explains displacement — floating ice already displaces its weight so melting holds the level, while land ice adds new water — maps the cryosphere as a connected store (~69% of fresh water) and transfers to a new case (Greenland vs Arctic sea ice).
responseLevels.partial: Knows land-ice melt raises the sea and can name several cryosphere parts, but lists them without the displacement reason; can't explain WHY floating ice is different.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two big ice cubes are melting. One is floating in a glass of water filled right to the brim. The other is sitting on a saucer next to the glass. When both have melted, which one — if either — makes water spill over the edge of the glass? Tell me which, and then tell me WHY.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding 'any melting ice raises sea level' says the floating cube overflows the glass; the child who distinguishes floating (displacement) from land ice says only the saucer ice adds water. The reason-tier forces displacement reasoning, not 'more water = higher'.
